video_title: Software vs. Semis: The Next Battle in AI | Protect the Pile Episode 26
gist: A free-form September 18th conversation between Hedgeye Asset Management's Patrick Kent (RPK) and portfolio manager co-host Sam, arguing that the market is effectively a one-factor (oil) model: diesel at ~$6.50/gal (up to ~$10 in California), physical crude near $120 versus ~$105 forward Brent, a hawkish Fed hiking into a rate-of-change peak, the 10-year at ~5%, and triple-C spreads at 920bp. The software-vs-semis 'battle' in the title is one segment of a much broader discussion: they argue three-month momentum has flipped to software while 12-month momentum is still stale semis, that both baskets can work into year-end, and that memory pricing has likely passed its tight peak on Chinese capacity. The back half covers AI safety as regulatory capture/PR cover for physical buildout limits, value accruing to the app layer rather than frontier closed-weight models, Apple's missing Vision Pro killer app, and a coming shakeout where hyperscalers buy distressed neocloud capacity and permits.

insights.claim: With the S&P 500 around 7620-7625 and only about 2% off its all-time high, only roughly 30-35% of names are above their 50-day moving average, meaning the headline index level is masking substantial internal deterioration.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Narrow breadth near highs is a classic setup for index-level vulnerability; watch percent-above-50-day as the tell rather than the index print.
insights.quote: there's roughly 30 to 35% of names above the 50-day moving average or the moving monkey as we uh lovingly call it around here

insights.claim: High yield has flipped to a bearish trend, the BB-to-Treasury spread sits around 273 basis points after widening roughly 20bp in a month, and the triple-C spread is at 920bp — implying a ~14% all-in borrowing cost for the weakest issuers.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Triple-C is where private-equity portfolio credit actually lives, so a 920bp spread is a direct stress reading on PE marks and refinancing capacity.
insights.quote: so for those following at home, that's a 14% cost to borrow on the crappiest companies and uh those crappy companies are what your PE credit looks like

insights.claim: Consumer-exposed equities have almost no names left on bullish trend signals, with consumer relative strength versus the market deteriorating continuously since spring.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK) and Sam, co-hosts
insights.so_what: A near-total absence of bullish consumer names argues against the 'resilient consumer' narrative and favors staying short or underweight discretionary.
insights.quote: boying consumer it's just a blood bath. I mean it is like there are very few names left that um are bullish trend

insights.claim: Financials and industrials — consensus long positions for much of the year — have been hit in recent weeks as yields declined and oil prices climbed, part of a broader rotation and narrowing of the market.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Crowded consensus longs unwinding is a source of forced selling; monitor whether the rotation is churn or the start of a broader de-risking.

insights.claim: Hedge fund and long-only positioning data from Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley shows light exposure — particularly in the momentum basket — with substantial cash on the sidelines waiting for a directional signal.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Light positioning plus dry powder is the bull case: 'less bad' headlines that relieve crude pressure could be enough to trigger a chase without any fundamental resolution.

insights.claim: The dollar has turned bullish on Hedgeye's signal following the hawkish Fed meeting, which tightens global dollar liquidity and slows the speakers' liquidity index.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: A bullish dollar plus a hawkish Fed is a double squeeze on global liquidity — a headwind for risk assets and emerging markets regardless of the equity index level.

insights.claim: The current equity market is effectively a one-factor model driven by crude oil: futures rally when oil falls, and the 10-year yield near 5% is being held up primarily by oil-driven inflation concern rather than fiscal or growth factors.
insights.speaker: Sam and Patrick Kent (RPK), co-hosts
insights.so_what: If one variable explains most of the tape, position sizing and hedging should be built around crude rather than around diversified macro scenarios.
insights.quote: if you really boil it down this this market is a one factor model market

insights.claim: Physical crude is trading near $120 while forward Brent is around $105 on a contract that rolls within about a week, and that gap must converge — creating a structural bullish cushion under oil prices.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: The physical-forward spread is a mechanical upside risk to futures into the roll; fading oil purely on headlines ignores the convergence math.
insights.quote: So either the physical market has to come down to this price or that the price is going to grind higher.

insights.claim: WTI's trend-line signal sits in the mid-90s, so crude could fall from over $100 to the mid-to-high $90s and still register as signal-bullish, making any such decline a false relief rally rather than a regime change.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete level: don't treat a drop to the mid-90s as a green light — the bearish oil trade only confirms below the trend line.

insights.claim: Diesel is the tightest point of the energy complex at roughly $6.50 a gallon nationally and around $10 in places like California, with spot station-level sellouts that a futures price decline would not physically resolve for days or weeks.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK) and Sam, co-hosts
insights.so_what: Diesel scarcity, not the crude screen price, is the binding constraint on freight, industrial activity and construction — track physical availability, not the futures curve.

insights.claim: Refineries are being run flat out without normal maintenance turnarounds because of product shortages, and Exxon has already brought a diesel refinery down — layering mechanical failure risk on top of an active hurricane season in a system with no slack.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: In a maximally tight system, small operational failures cascade — refinery outage risk is an underpriced tail for diesel cracks and headline inflation.
insights.quote: when you don't maintain a refinery, it blows up

insights.claim: A proposed administration ban on refined product exports would at best knock diesel from around $6.50 to $6.00 briefly and does not address the underlying supply shortage.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK) and Sam, co-hosts
insights.so_what: Fade any sustained bearish energy repricing on export-ban headlines; the policy is cosmetic relative to the physical deficit.

insights.claim: Oil has shifted from being an inflationary force to the point of demand destruction, and prices this elevated should become a disinflationary force as companies and consumers cut fuel and other wallet spending — showing up in the data in 2027.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Frames the trade sequence: long inflation now, but the 2027 setup is disinflation via demand destruction — which would invalidate hawkish Fed pricing.

insights.claim: JP Morgan's commodities team publicly withdrew its forecast, and the speakers argue that is the intellectually correct response to a tightly coupled multivariate system rather than a failure worth mocking.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: When sell-side research abandons point forecasts, follow price signals over narrative — a process argument for trend-following in commodities right now.
insights.quote: why do you feel so confident in a complex multivariate system where there's all kinds of cascading effects?

insights.claim: Momentum is a rotating basket of companies rather than a sector, so its constituents change over time — meaning a momentum exposure can silently become a bet on an entirely different set of businesses.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Investors holding momentum products need to re-underwrite holdings on every rebalance; factor exposure is not stable sector exposure.
insights.quote: momentum is not a sector, right? It's a basket of companies.

insights.claim: On three-month momentum software is now dominating, while on the classic 12-month-minus-one-month long-wave measure semiconductor names still sit at the top but are falling down the rankings — a direct tug-of-war between short-wave and long-wave momentum definitions.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: The horizon you use determines whether you are long software or long semis right now; the rebalance mechanics themselves are a flow catalyst.
insights.quote: depending on how you're defining momentum, it's like there's this tugof-war between you want shortwave or longer wave momentum

insights.claim: The standard naive momentum construction ranks stocks on trailing 12-month returns excluding the most recent month, deliberately dropping the last month so recent pullbacks are not penalized — which is precisely why the July-peaking AI hardware names still occupy the long-wave basket.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Explains the lag: stale AI hardware winners stay in quant momentum baskets for months after they top, creating a mechanical supply of future selling.

insights.claim: The 'AI will put software out of business' narrative has broken down, with the market now separating software losers from companies with defensible moats, driving a software recovery off extinction-level positioning.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: The positioning base is so low that software can re-rate substantially on nothing more than the absence of disruption, independent of earnings acceleration.
insights.quote: positioning has improved, but it's improved from rock bottom, you know, you know, extin extinction levels

insights.claim: Software and semiconductors can both work simultaneously into year-end: software has the three-month momentum tailwind plus receding extinction risk, while semis have light positioning and beta that investors may chase — absent negative AI headlines.
insights.speaker: Sam and Patrick Kent (RPK), co-hosts
insights.so_what: Argues against the either/or framing that has driven pair trades all year; a broad tech rally is possible and would squeeze software/semis pair positions.

insights.claim: The real resolution is that the have/have-not divide stops being semis versus software and becomes haves and have-nots within each group, with the all-in bid scrubbed out of the weaker names in both baskets.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Shifts the trade from sector-level to single-name dispersion — favors long/short within tech over directional sector bets.

insights.claim: Memory is a commodity business with Chinese DRAM capacity expanding, so peak pricing tightness in memory has probably already passed regardless of whether Western buyers purchase Chinese product, because it is a global price.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: A direct short thesis on memory names: the 'we don't buy Chinese' defense is irrelevant to global pricing, same as steel.
insights.quote: memory is a commodity business that the Chinese are expanding capacity in

insights.claim: Intel is arguably the single best-positioned company for a US semiconductor manufacturing footprint because it already has fab capacity built that needs to be filled, and its signal is improving.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: A reshoring-policy call option distinct from the AI-compute trade; existing idle fab capacity is the asymmetry.

insights.claim: Within software, Adobe remains a loser while Snowflake and Twilio are in genuinely good competitive positions, with Twilio's narrative fully changed and its valuation described as not that demanding.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Names specific long candidates that could migrate into and stay in the momentum basket, versus a named avoid.
insights.quote: Adobe still sucks

insights.claim: The 2021 software blowup is the template for what happens next in AI hardware: peak multiples layered on peak fundamentals mean-revert violently when the second derivative shifts, combining multiple compression with slowing estimate revisions.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: The double-whammy of multiple mean reversion plus revision cuts is the mechanism to watch in semis, not a valuation call in isolation.
insights.quote: you're sitting here at peak on peak multiple like that's an ugly setup

insights.claim: By 2027 the speakers expect a broader basket of surviving software names and a narrower basket of semiconductor and AI hardware names than consensus assumed at the start of the year, because the rate-of-change comps facing memory and semis are too large to comp against regardless of multiple.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: A concrete 2027 allocation shift: widen software exposure, concentrate semis into a small set of genuine survivors.

themes.theme: Fed and the Capex Cost Squeeze

insights.claim: The Fed raised rates at its Wednesday meeting despite odds markets already pricing a 90% chance, and the hosts believe policy is hiking directly into what will prove to be a cycle peak in rate of change.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Hiking into a decelerating economy is the classic policy error setup; positions should anticipate rapid repricing of the 2027 path.

insights.claim: Market-implied 2027 Fed hike expectations are unreliable and likely to be erased, because rates cannot fix an oil supply shortage and the only channel available is curbing demand enough to slow the economy.
insights.speaker: Sam and Patrick Kent (RPK), co-hosts
insights.so_what: Directly tradeable: fade priced 2027 hikes, since the Fed's tool cannot address supply-side energy inflation without triggering the slowdown that removes the hikes.
insights.quote: I got to believe those are like in fake pencil that could be easily erased

insights.claim: Data center capex is now being underwritten at peak input prices across the board — steel, copper, diesel and memory all elevated — so builders are taking an unusually large gamble on returns even before demand risk is considered.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Input-cost inflation degrades project IRRs mechanically; a pause in capex is far more likely at these cost levels than models assume.
insights.quote: you're not only building the capex but you're building it at peak prices for everything

insights.claim: Data center capex is now the single biggest driver of industrial activity at the margin, so even a modest capex pause — triggered by high diesel prices or input scarcity — would produce a sharp second-derivative slowdown in industrial rate of change.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Ties an energy-cost shock directly to industrial earnings; consistent with Keith McCullough's ETF Pro carrying industrial momentum as a short.

themes.theme: AI Safety Narrative as Regulatory Capture

insights.claim: The coordinated AI safety push is best read as a PR and regulatory-capture campaign designed to fence off a small set of trusted incumbents from open-source and emerging model competitors rather than as a genuine risk disclosure.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK) and Sam, co-hosts
insights.so_what: If regulatory capture succeeds it is a moat for closed-weight incumbents; if the pushback holds, open-source economics win — a binary worth tracking for AI equity exposure.

insights.claim: The safety campaign compressed Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, the New York Times, and METR — a monitoring body affiliated with Anthropic and effective altruism — plus politically embedded activists into a three-day window, which the hosts read as evidence of coordination and lobbying spend rather than organic concern.
insights.speaker: Sam and Patrick Kent (RPK), co-hosts
insights.so_what: Reads as a deepseek-style narrative shock; such episodes have historically been buying opportunities in AI-levered names once the coordination is exposed.

insights.claim: A second, unstated motive for the 'slow down' narrative is that data center and utility capex is hitting hard physical and regulatory limits — permitting, inspections, town meetings — that make sustained 20-30% growth rates impossible, so a safety rationale is more flattering than admitting capacity constraints.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Implies AI infrastructure growth decelerates for physical reasons regardless of demand — a ceiling that capex forecasts do not model.
insights.quote: as soon as all the like the lowhanging stuff is gone, you're up against just the physics of not being able to grow this any quicker

insights.claim: A third driver is mounting legal liability, exemplified by reports of Anthropic-built agents hacking OpenAI emails, which the hosts see as the opening of a large and growing open liability from rogue agent behavior.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Agent liability is an unpriced cost line for model companies and their enterprise customers; watch for insurance and indemnification terms emerging.
insights.quote: we probably cause ourselves more problems with AI long before AI gives us problems

insights.claim: Existing regulatory bodies including the FTC have overseen product liability and consumer protection for a century, so new AI-specific regulation is unnecessary — a pushback argument that gained traction quickly against the safety push.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Suggests the capture attempt may fail, keeping open-source competition alive and capping the moat premium in closed-model valuations.

themes.theme: Where AI Value Accrues: Apps, Distribution and Devices

insights.claim: The bulk of real-world AI productivity gains will come from lightweight models running on proprietary enterprise data — a law firm training on its own history rather than the whole internet — not from the next frontier closed-weight model.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: If true, the ROI accrues to data owners and vertical application vendors, not to whoever wins the frontier-model race — a direct challenge to capex-driven valuations.
insights.quote: I'm not an AI skeptic, I'm an AI claim skeptic

insights.claim: Over 90% of token consumption goes to basic and semi-basic queries while roughly 10% uses cutting-edge models for heavy research workloads, and margins and profitability are skewed toward that small high-end slice.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Volume and profit pools sit in different places in AI — revenue-per-token assumptions built on blended volume will overstate economics.
insights.quote: it is a large number like 90 plus% of token consumption goes for really basic semi-basic queries

insights.claim: The iOS/Android split is the right framework for AI model economics: Android holds roughly 60-70% of global unit share while Apple captures roughly 60-70% of the profit pie, and AI model usage will likely skew even further in that direction.
insights.speaker: Sam and Patrick Kent (RPK), co-hosts
insights.so_what: Provides a valuation anchor: open models can win share while a small number of closed players still take most of the profit, so unit-share data is not the investable metric.

insights.claim: Coding via Codex and Claude Code has been the light-bulb enterprise application driving token consumption, but no comparable consumer application yet exists that tangibly changes ordinary users' lives.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: The AI revenue base is narrower than the capex implies; a consumer killer app arriving is the catalyst that would validate the spending, and its absence is the bear case.

insights.claim: Meta's new consumer AI device/app is the first genuinely high-utility, zero-friction consumer AI product the hosts have used, though privacy concerns about granting Meta full access remain the main adoption hurdle.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: First-hand adoption signal on Meta as the likely consumer AI distribution winner; privacy friction is the variable that determines penetration.

insights.claim: Meta's Threads launch demonstrates the company's consumer distribution power and its limits: it ramped extremely fast when X sentiment was sour, faded to a distant number two once X recovered, and is now sustained by cross-traffic from Instagram taps.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Distribution gets a product in front of consumers instantly but does not create retention — the test for Meta's AI app is whether utility, not reach, holds users.

insights.claim: Meta, Apple and to a lesser extent Google hold the decisive advantage in AI because value will accrue at the application layer, and they are rarely first but consistently ship high-utility products on top of someone else's compute.
insights.speaker: Sam and Patrick Kent (RPK), co-hosts
insights.so_what: Argues for owning consumer distribution platforms over pure model companies as the durable AI exposure.

insights.claim: The closed-weight 'platform to end all platforms' race between OpenAI and Anthropic may be a backward-looking replication of the old internet consolidation model, when the actual outcome this time could be fragmentation.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the winner-take-all premise underpinning frontier-lab valuations; a fragmented outcome would compress those valuations severely.

insights.claim: Like the dot-com era, the AI bubble can burst while the applications it seeded — the equivalents of Amazon, eBay and Priceline — go on to define consumer and enterprise behavior for decades.
insights.speaker: Sam and Patrick Kent (RPK), co-hosts
insights.so_what: Separates the asset-price call from the technology call: being right on AI's durability says nothing about surviving the drawdown.
insights.quote: the the the it seeded the the consumer and enterprise behavior for the the following decades to come

insights.claim: Vision Pro has undersold because Apple never built a compelling use case, and a live NBA courtside package at roughly a $2,000 annual subscription would sell millions of units by itself.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: A concrete, currently-unpriced revenue path for Apple hardware; Apple partnering with a major sports league would be the signal to re-rate the device franchise.

insights.claim: The adjacent Vision Pro content opportunities are large and specific: Live Nation front-row concerts, IMAX films at home, NHL on-the-glass seats, and premium tennis finals seats like the US Open, sellable globally at prices far below physical tickets.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK) and Sam, co-hosts
insights.so_what: Names potential partner beneficiaries — a Live Nation or IMAX deal would be an early tell on this thesis materializing.

insights.claim: The iPod is the template: Apple was not first to the MP3 player and the device was incidental — the iTunes store was the actual product, and Vision Pro currently lacks that ecosystem layer.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: A reusable test for any new hardware category: evaluate the content/ecosystem deal flow, not the device specifications.
insights.quote: there's no point introducing a device that doesn't have a use case

themes.theme: Data Center Credit, Power and the Coming Shakeout

insights.claim: AI buildout credit demand will increasingly compete with sovereign borrowing globally, and credit investors will start explicitly comparing developed-market sovereign paper against Amazon or Google corporate credit in allocation meetings.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: A structural crowding-out risk for Treasury issuance costs and a re-rating catalyst for hyperscaler spreads; the tell is when a corporate borrows through the sovereign.
insights.quote: that'll be the indicator when they can borrow at better rates

insights.claim: Hyperscalers will frontload as much data center spending as possible before the end of 2028 because the presidential election could change the regulatory and policy equation entirely, even though permitting, power, and labor constraints are rate-limiting steps.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Implies a capex pull-forward through 2028 followed by a cliff — the opposite of the smooth multi-year ramp embedded in supplier estimates.

insights.claim: Speculative neocloud data center builders financed by lower-quality credit will follow the internet buildout template — bankruptcy or the pink sheets — with their capacity ultimately bought cheaply by the well-capitalized players, just as AT&T and Verizon absorbed the independents.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Short the levered spec builders, and treat distress in that cohort as an asset-acquisition catalyst for the hyperscalers rather than a sector-wide negative.
insights.quote: they'll end up owning a bunch of this capacity that's been built on spec by less like credit quality players

insights.claim: Texas is triaging a multi-gigawatt power interconnection backlog by categorizing requests into batches based on financing legitimacy, local approval progress and backup power, leaving a long tail of mom-and-pop developers who will never be connected.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Headline interconnection queue numbers massively overstate real data center demand; the triaged batch-zero list is the number that matters for power and equipment demand.

insights.claim: A Bernstein chart showed that an outsized share of incremental data center announcements came from fly-by-night speculative builders rather than credible operators.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Announced-capacity pipelines are a poor proxy for real spending; discount the announcement-driven demand estimates supporting AI supply-chain forecasts.

insights.claim: Permits themselves will become the acquirable asset — hyperscalers unable to get their own approvals will simply buy permitted projects off distressed developers, since unlike the developers they have no debt-driven urgency to build immediately.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: Identifies where residual value sits in failing neoclouds — permits and interconnection rights, not the physical assets.

insights.claim: Contractors and suppliers will prioritize name-brand, fully-financed buyers — Amazon, Blackstone, Brookfield and KKR — leaving smaller developers unable to secure supply contract capacity at any price.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Supply chain access, not capital alone, is the real barrier to entry in data centers — a durable moat for the largest sponsors.
insights.quote: Amazon, Blackstone, Brookfield, K, all these guys are going to gobble up that that supply contract capacity.

insights.claim: A 6% deficit with no recession, no slowdown and no exogenous COVID-like shock is the genuinely alarming fact, because the interest-payment share of the budget grows from there with no obvious escape from the math.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kent (RPK), Hedgeye Asset Management
insights.so_what: This is the structural gold-bull argument; with the 10-year near 5% it becomes a live bond-market risk rather than a decade-out concern.

insights.claim: If Democrats win the House in the midterms, the purse effectively closes for two years with little new spending outside emergency items like defense.
insights.speaker: Sam, co-host and portfolio manager
insights.so_what: Gridlock caps fiscal impulse into 2027-28, removing a growth support just as energy-driven demand destruction bites.
